This study introduces H-STREAM, an analytical pipeline designed to manage continuous streams of data and query massive historical datasets. Developed as a complementary flow to the Stream Processing Language Engine (SPLOS) platform, H-STREAM integrates with the H-Base distributed storage system. It features a comprehensive suite of operators covering stream processing basics, advanced functions like windowing and buffering, query capabilities, and machine learning tools. The system features a modular architecture that supports distributed operators capable of scaling across multiple compute and storage nodes. Evaluation results indicate that H-STREAM delivers significant performance gains and cost reductions when compared to assembling standard data flow components from existing big data software packages.

Investigating the mechanisms of supersymmetry breaking alongside the Higgs boson mass generation problem has led to the hypothesis of extra partners for the Standard Model's fundamental particles. Specifically, the discovery of vector-like top and bottom partners at high-mass scales could offer a non-minimal solution to the Higgs mass puzzle. This study analyzes both resonant and non-resonant cross-sections for single-production scenarios of these partners at a 14 TeV proton-proton collider. We identify three distinct non-resonant diagrams involving the interaction of a quark-antiquark pair with the creation of a top partner and its superpartner (or bottom partner and its superpartner in different BSM contexts). Notably, in certain kinematic regions where kinematic thresholds are satisfied and detector acceptance allows, these non-resonant contributions can be comparable to the resonant ones. Consequently, these non-resonant processes must be incorporated into any rigorous collider search strategy for such particles.

Neural machine translation (NMT) systems utilizing SPARQL queries operate by decoding sequences to generate SPARQL statements that execute queries over a knowledge base (KB). These models rely on a special "query" token to initiate elements, such as those found in a SELECT clause. However, this single token must represent all instances of any given KB feature—for example, it must be able to denote "title" in both "select title from ... where title='A'" and "select title from ... where title='B'". Consequently, distinguishing between different instances becomes impossible, leading to incorrect model predictions. To resolve this limitation, we introduce a copy mechanism that enables the model to accurately handle entities from the knowledge base without relying solely on the generic query token. Our approach is straightforward to integrate and delivers substantial performance improvements.

Scholarship metrics serve as a primary method for gauging the quality of a research group, a paper, or a specific venue. While recent efforts increasingly evaluate papers based on their venue rather than individual citations, such approaches often fail to accurately reflect quality for three key reasons: first, top-tier venues frequently attract significant attention due to high intrinsic quality, creating a feedback loop that inflates metrics regardless of actual contribution; second, attention can be driven by transient research trends that do not necessarily correlate with quality; third, current metrics often struggle to capture the nuanced attention a paper may deserve. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Venue Quality (VQ), a new metric designed specifically to measure venue quality independently. VQ is derived entirely from user engagement data on Google Scholar, specifically utilizing click-through rates to reflect genuine interest without relying on citation counts. The authors demonstrate that VQ effectively correlates with human quality assessments for both venues and individual papers, successfully outperforming existing venue-based metrics in distinguishing quality effectively.

Neural networks have become a standard tool in modern controller design, yet their guarantee of safety under all circumstances is not established. Addressing this gap, this study focuses on formal verification for neural network controllers within stochastic systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations. The approach formulates safety checking as an optimization task, which is then relaxed into a differentiable problem suitable for back-propagation-based solvers. The paper also covers verification scenarios involving discrete feedforward networks and networks with one hidden layer, demonstrating their practical utility through numerical examples.

This study introduces a functorial framework for overdetermined hierarchical clustering. The method is designed to be robust, straightforward to implement, and effective at capturing intricate information flows within intricate datasets. In contrast to standard algorithms that typically generate a binary dendrogram, this approach creates an overdetermined clustering structure where each node encompasses a broad spectrum of similarities among its children. Furthermore, the proposed method is insensitive to re-labeling and can be executed in linear time. Finally, we provide a rigorous mathematical formulation of the algorithm and demonstrate its efficacy through a simulation based on the Starburst dataset.

Tensor completion techniques are widely utilized for reconstructing visual data in scenarios involving significant corruption or missing entries. Nevertheless, real-world applications often involve high-resolution data that cannot be effectively managed using batch processing. This study introduces a novel approach for real-time, streaming reconstruction of high-resolution visual datasets characterized by sparse noise and data loss. The proposed framework initially segments high-resolution images into patches, which are then fed sequentially into a streaming algorithm. This algorithm employs tensor ring completion adapted with specific tracking mechanisms to ensure patches are accurately reconstructed in their original spatial context. Furthermore, to enhance both computational efficiency and potential for one-step recovery, a regularization term based on the generalized total variation (s-variation) is integrated into the optimization model. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets confirm that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both perpatch and holistic image reconstruction.

This study employs numerical simulations to investigate energy spectrum $E(k)$ of inertial waves characterized by wavenumber $k$ and wavenumber-dependent frequency $\omega(k)$ in periodic three-dimensional space. The spectrum remains constant over an intermediate wavenumber range within two distinct models: the isotropic Boussinesq approximation and a rotation-inclusive model. These models were run under conditions of either isotropic or axisymmetric (unified) excitation. In both scenarios, the Isard-Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectrum was identified, demonstrating that this classic inertial wave turbulence model is not constrained to the Boussinesq approximation.

This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of gate-modulated monolayer graphene by leveraging universal thermodynamic relationships and ensuring consistency with established theoretical models. We demonstrate that low-temperature entropy in such electrically controlled systems exhibits a universal dependency on the product of layer capacitance ($C_g$) and room-temperature gate voltage ($V_g$). Furthermore, we establish that low-temperature specific heat in gate-modulated graphene follows a universal function of $C_gV_g/T$, which scales with the Bessel function order. We also derive analytical expressions for internal energy, entropy, and specific heat, which are subsequently verified against recent experimental findings. Notably, we identify a distinct peak in entropy occurring near room-temperature ($\approx 300$ K) and a corresponding maximum in specific heat at a temperature of approximately $300$ K ($\approx 300$ K), both of which are found to be independent of the layer capacitance. These findings offer new avenues for exploring the thermal behavior of two-dimensional materials under external electrostatic modulation.

This study details a low-frequency (3--10 MHz) study of the binary system CR Dra, a binary system consisting of flare stars with spectral classes of K0V and M1V. The observations reveal a complex radio spectrum that exhibits both continuum emission and intermittent maser bursts. The continuum radiation is attributed to flare events from the M1V star, while maser bursts are linked to the K0V star. The detected maser emission spans the 3--10 MHz range, indicating that the magnetic field intensity of the source region is approximately 0.01 Gauss. Theoretical models demonstrate that electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) emission can reproduce the observed characteristics of these bursts, specifically their duration and variability. Furthermore, the analysis of the calculated ECM source regions shows that the observed variations in position angle and circular polarization are consistent with rotational modulation caused by the K0V star orbiting the M1V star.

Creating high-fidelity 3D virtual humans is vital for immersive social networking, gaming, and teleconferencing. Although current virtual avatars are already engaging, they lack essential features required by advanced applications, specifically the realistic portrayal of skeletal-driven movements and reactions to environmental stimuli. We introduce ARTIR, a system dedicated to rendering high-quality 3D avatars by integrating a high-fidelity texture synthesis engine with a physically-based model for articulated rendering. This rendering architecture supports real-time performance even at close viewing distances. To ensure high-quality detail, our novel framework employs ANR, a framework dedicated to generating detailed textures from lower-resolution images. This approach utilizes deep learning to enhance specific textural elements, overcome distortions, and rectify artifacts found in initial images. We have evaluated the system on two extensive datasets, demonstrating its ability to produce superior imagery compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Human and machine intelligence differ in numerous significant ways. This paper specifically investigates how mild to moderate, and occasionally severe, image transformations are perceived by machines versus humans. Although machines and humans often diverge in their responses to such spatial changes, the frequency and nature of these differences require clarification. Our study presents two primary contributions: (1) two extensive datasets comprising 15,360 images and 102,450 human-labeled annotations, and (2) a comprehensive analysis demonstrating distinct patterns of disagreement between human and machine perception across various spatial transformations.

This study explores the interplay between Askey-Wilson algebras, Chern-Simons (CS) theory, and link invariants. Initially, we briefly outline how to construct quantum spin representations for the Askey-Wilson algebras and subsequently analyze their role within. Subsequently, a three-dimensional CS theory is set up to render these Askey-Wilson algebras via their central extensions, facilitating a transition from these algebras to quantum spin representations of the Hecke algebras $H_n$. Transitioning to physics, we utilize a Chern-Simons framework to derive quantum spin representations of $H_n$ out of those belonging to the Askey-Wilson algebras, thereby linking them to link invariants. Furthermore, we examine how this transition from Askey-Wilson algebras to Hecke algebras $H_n$ impacts link invariants, noting that these topological invariants are tied to the Askey-Wilson algebras through their central extensions. Consequently, we establish a correspondence where Askey-Wilson algebras map to Hecke algebras $H_n$ within the context of quantum spin representations, thereby associating these structures with specific link invariants.

Large-scale pre-trained models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance, though it remains unclear whether their performance on specific tasks aligns with their practical utility. This study introduces the concept of Dataset Collections (COLs) and Collection-based Prompts (CPs)—which leverage syntactic structures found across multiple tasks—to investigate zero-shot generalization across various domains and categories of the Civil Service Exams (CSE) dataset. By evaluating various large language models (LLMs) using these specialized prompts and input configurations, we benchmark their effectiveness. Furthermore, we explore the potential benefits of meta-tuning LLMs on such collections to enhance performance. Our findings reveal that while current off-the-shelf LLMs struggle with zero-shot generalization on Pseudo-synthetic CSE datasets, they can be effectively adapted through simple prompt optimizations. Additionally, the paper presents a strategy for constructing high-quality answer templates for zero-shot tasks, which significantly boosts model accuracy.

We examine the potential for detecting gravitational waves from a GW detector like LIGO, specifically within the context of an electroweak phase transition in the two-Higgs doublet model. The study focuses on scenarios where the transition occurs via a first-order mechanism, potentially serving as a signature of electroweak symmetry breaking. Constraints from collider experiments and dark matter searches are taken into account to narrow down viable parameter regions. The analysis reveals that first-order phase transitions can produce a significant signal detectable by current gravitational wave observatories. The implications of these findings for future collider experiments and gravitational wave detectors are also discussed.

We introduce an automated, interactive redshift estimation tool named "High-z Sudoku" designed for use with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Leveraging the principles of interstellar medium Sudoku puzzles, this tool cross-references molecular emission lines against a comprehensive catalog to identify spectroscopic features and calculate redshifts. Its utility extends to various ALMA observational modes, including continuum, spectral line, and spectral line+continuum surveys. We emphasize that High-z Sudoku serves as a powerful diagnostic instrument for verifying the reliability of redshift measurements derived from individual line spectra, particularly in the early universe. Additionally, it can be employed to determine the redshift distribution of (sub)millimeter continuum sources within high-redshift surveys. We provide a detailed description of the tool's operation and its implementation interface, along with a set of test cases to demonstrate its effectiveness.

After detailing the dynamical structure factor's (DSSF) behavior across various phases—namely the gapped symmetry-broken, critical, and disordered regimes—we present a universal method to identify them. This approach relies on calculating the total entropy of the DSSF, denoted $S_{DSSF}$, within the lowest excitation spectra. By analyzing $S_{DSSF}$, one can pinpoint the onset of the disordered phase, observe criticality, and determine the gap size in the symmetry-broken phase. Specifically, $S_{DSSF}$ rises monotonically with the number of lowest excitations included; a jump in monotonicity signals the disordered phase, while a peak indicates criticality. Within the $Z_3$ ordered phase, $S_{DSSF}$ increases with magnetization, where its gap behavior serves as a definitive marker for that phase. We find that for the lowest 160 magnons, $S_{DSSF}$ remains at approximately $\pi^2/4$ throughout the disordered phase, matching the limit of a collection of $N$ independent magnons. This study examines an $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills-like theory extended with $N_f=3$ Dirac quarks and $N_h=3$ Majorana Higgs fermons, all transforming as the adjoint representation of $SU(3)$. The analysis investigates vacuum properties by evaluating the fundamental and wedge loop loops across the full range of quark and Higgs masses, with particular focus on the boundary between confined and deconfined states. The findings indicate a broad region in the phase diagram where confinement prevails, encompassing scenarios with massive or massless quarks and Higgs. Furthermore, when at least one massless species (either a quark or Higgs) is present, there is no distinct deconfined phase; instead, the system transitions continuously to a deconfined state characterized by critical exponents that align with the 3-dimensional Ising universality class.

The tetragonal intermetallic Cr$_2$Al exhibits antiferromagnetic ordering at a transition temperature of $T_{\rm N} = 115$ K, featuring two distinct types of antiferromagnetic coupling: one within the Al-induced nearest-neighbor Cr–Cr pairs and another between more distant, direct-neighbor Cr–Cr pairs. The latter, which connects Cr atoms situated on the same $a$-$c$ plane, is significantly stronger than the former. This weaker coupling links Cr atoms across different $a$-$c$ planes via an indirect superexchange pathway that includes Al $p$-orbitals. Furthermore, our findings reveal a pronounced anisotropy in the coupling strengths along the $a$ and $c$ directions, which can be attributed to the specific characteristics of Al $p$-orbitals.

This study investigates rarefied gas flows by utilizing the Unified Gas-kinetic Theory (UGKT) combined with a model featuring velocity-dependent collision frequencies. Through the derivation of this new kinetic model and the development of appropriate boundary conditions, we analyze rarefied flows under various molecular mechanisms by adjusting the velocity-dependent exponent parameter. Results indicate that when the exponent is set to 1.0, the resulting flow fields align closely with those produced by hard-sphere kinetics, whereas other exponent values result in flow characteristics distinctively unlike hard-sphere behavior. Specifically, we identify that an exponent of 1.2 corresponds to the most realistic representation of monatomic gas flows, reflecting the actual intermolecular potential. Consequently, this simple velocity-dependent framework offers a more accurate and efficient method for simulating real gas flows compared to traditional hard-sphere kinetic theory.

We study the challenge of parsing natural language to produce structured representations, specifically targeting tasks like coreference resolution and meaning extraction. While recent advances utilizing neural architectures and natural language input have yielded significant progress, these methods typically depend on large-scale datasets. In contrast, many practical applications are constrained to scenarios involving limited training data. This paper addresses few-shot natural language parsing. We introduce a novel approach that leverages pre-trained language models to derive both natural language input and the corresponding structural components directly from unlabelled corpora. Experiments on various datasets and environments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques relying on token embeddings, particularly in regimes with scarce labelled data.

The next generation of hadron and nuclear colliders, planned for the 2030s, aims to deliver some of the most precise measurements of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) ever undertaken. These objectives necessitate particle detectors with superior tracking capabilities to achieve high-resolution momentum measurements, precise vertexing, and excellent impact parameter resolution. To fulfill these requirements, both facilities will feature state-of-the-art, planar silicon pixel detectors designed to handle extremely high radiation environments. This document reviews the progress made toward constructing such systems for the Electron-Ion Collider, drawing upon lessons learned from previous projects like LHCb, ALICE, and LHC upgrades. Additionally, it examines the potential for using thin, lightweight silicon detectors in collider environments and explores the future research required to realize this concept.

The study of magnetic fields in main-sequence stars is essential for understanding their internal structure, evolution, and activity cycles. This case analysis focuses on HD58260, a rapidly rotating B9.5V star, which exhibits significant spectral emission from the upper chromosphere and chromosphere. By utilizing emission lines in this region, researchers can detect variations in the radial magnetic field across chanced height differences. This work presents spectropolarimetric data collected by IRTF/INMAD on HD58260 during its maximum rotation rate. The findings confirm a strong surface magnetic field alongside a measurable gradient through the outer atmospheric layers. The observed gradient aligns with current theoretical models regarding the generation mechanism of this gradient, specifically the Tayler-Spruit dynamo.

It is demonstrated that an $n=1d$ representation of the intertwining operator, belonging to the differential and $\hbar$-rotation group, admits free boson realization. Consequently, representations of the intertwining operator, special linear group and general linear group, can be derived from the free Schrödinger field. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence linking the free Schrödinger field to the free boson theory, and free boson to free fermion, for every integer power of the oscillator number. Utilizing this framework, we determine the two-point correlation functions within the Schrödinger field. Additionally, by integrating the algebraic structure inherent in the Dunkl operators, we identify a probabilistic interpretation of the intertwining operator, identifying it as a stochastic skew-symmetric random walk. In this probabilistic setup, the parameters of the random walk correspond to those of the integrable system associated with the affine Weyl algebra for rank 1, specifically the $A_1^{(1)}$ model.

We present 1.2 mm ALMA observations of H$_3$0$\alpha$ emission in the low metallicity galaxy NGC 5253, a choice made specifically because the H$_3$0$\alpha$ line is far less sensitive to dust obscuration than Pa$\alpha$. The study reveals a strong correlation between H$_3$0$\alpha$ and Pa$\alpha$ fluxes across the galaxy, and a comparison with the well-studied CO(3-2) line shows that both are spatially correlated, a relationship that remains robust even after correcting for extinction. We also examine the relationship among these three tracers and find that a model incorporating both extinction and variations in relative line strengths provides a superior fit compared to one relying solely on variable relative strengths. Additionally, we assess the efficacy of using H$_3$0$\alpha$ to estimate star formation rates by contrasting it with the H$\beta$ line. Our results demonstrate that the ratio of H$_3$0$\alpha$ to H$\beta$ is constant within NGC 5253, indicating that H$_3$0$\alpha$ can serve as a reliable star formation indicator in low metallicity galaxies like NGC 5253.

In this study, we investigate observer-based strategies for estimating the state of epidemic phenomena. Our work establishes the existence of an observer for a linear infection-susceptible model with observed total susceptible counts within a probabilistic framework where measurements are subject to noise. Furthermore, by addressing specific scenarios where measurement noise is negligible, we analyze both discrete and continuous epidemiological non-linear Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) and Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) models. Specifically, the discrete scenario employs zoom-and-rotate techniques coupled with high-gain observers to ensure local exponential convergence, while in the continuous context, contraction theory is utilized to demonstrate the existence of observers with guaranteed exponential convergence rates.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly utilized across diverse fields to capture real-world entity relationships. While static KG models have achieved significant success, they fail to account for temporal dynamics, an essential factor in many domains. Although incorporating time can enhance model performance, it often results in larger, more complex graphs that complicate learning and inference. This paper addresses the challenge of predicting temporal links efficiently. We introduce a heuristic that leverages time by employing a static model on a reduced graph, thereby lowering computational overhead. Our experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that this approach not only accelerates prediction speed but also outperforms both leading-state-of-the-art static models and specialized dynamic models for link prediction tasks.

Ultrashort pulses from ring-mode-locking laser systems have become essential for generating high-peak-power, fast transient radiation for nonlinear optical processes. This study presents a geometric analysis of astigmatism and mirror curvature in a ring-resonator setup, specifically tailored for Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML). We demonstrate that this approach enables the design of KLML oscillators operating at peak powers exceeding 100 GW. Furthermore, we examine the impact of intracavity elements on the dispersion matrix and the resultant pulse characteristics. Our findings indicate that strategic placement of a thin lens can reduce aperture astigmatism, allowing for a flat-end hollowed output beam that facilitates direct imaging onto a target.

As a prominent approach to distributed machine learning, asynchronous online federated learning (AOL) addresses the varying computational and communication constraints of clients by enabling them to participate in training based on their availability. Nevertheless, a significant limitation of AOL is its lack of explicit control over client participation, creating a risk where models may underperform or become biased if too many or too few devices join. To address this, we introduce an innovative asynchronous federated learning framework that learns a dynamic selection policy to guide which clients should join training at any moment. This policy is created using the readily accessible local data at each client, requiring no prior knowledge of other participants' data or communication capabilities. We validate this method through nonlinear regression experiments, utilizing real-world datasets and realistic simulations of client participation patterns. A prevalent approach to this problem is the Cumulant Expansion Technique (SET), which constructs an approximation for the superoperator mapping an initial observable $O(0)$ to its time-evolved counterpart $O(t)$. We introduce a generalized variant of SET designed specifically for matrices defined by equations involving several matrices rather than just a single system-Hamiltonian component in the equation of motion. Our methodology decomposes the superoperator into a sequence of shift operators that act on specific matrix entries within a supermatrix representation. By utilizing these operators within the cumulant expansion framework, we derive an algorithm capable of numerically approximating the superoperator. Our procedure encompasses established techniques such as the equation-of-motion SET and the self-energy SET as special cases. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical convergence characteristics of this new approach and assess its performance through applications involving both finite temperature spin models and zero-temperature photon systems.

This text presents a slice spectral sequence for a slice tower constructed from a sphincter version of the 3-dimensional quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum. Within this framework, the differentials correspond to the norm squaring operation acting on the graded algebra of 3-dimensional unit quaternions. The study establishes a final model for slice stable stems up to a specific filtration range and utilizes this model to confirm a version of the slice conjecture for those ranges.

Its degree provides a lower limit for the minimal number of generators in the parameter ideal defining the unmixed $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology of the associated ideal, while also reflecting the degree of the ring's tightness. Utilizing tightness analysis, the authors present fresh examples of $\mathfrak{m}$-reduced local rings that exhibit the property of being F-rational, F-singular, or simultaneously F-lifting and strongly F-regular under the property F-lifting and strongly F-regular under the property F-lifting. Machine learning models in radiology and digital pathology frequently utilize diverse file formats for image data, segmentation masks, and feature annotations. However, these standards often lack robust support for feature reporting or rely on inefficient, redundant file structures. Consequently, this research introduces **Highdicom**, a versatile open-source Python library designed to save image inputs alongside segmentation masks and feature metadata directly into single DICOM files according to the latest DICOM standards. Highdicom streamlines the development of new machine learning pipelines in radiology and pathology through a powerful segmentation API, batch-processing capabilities, and support for all relevant DICOM SOP classes. The software is released under the Apache License 2.0 and can be accessed at https://github.com/highdicom/highdicom.

This study derives the Noether current arising specifically from the surface contribution within the Einstein-Hilbert action. Demonstrating that this current aligns with the Belinfante form of the Hilbert energy-momentum tensor, it allows for the calculation of the corresponding radial components in canonical formalism; these components facilitate the application of the quantum consistency condition to derive the Bekenstein-Manning-Horrend entropy. Furthermore, utilizing these components provides a framework for evaluating the central charge within the theory, a result that satisfies the requirements imposed by the Virasoro algebra.

We evaluate supervised and unsupervised learning approaches for genomic DNA sequences, covering one-hot encoded single base pairs and sequences of nucleic acid bases. Our results indicate that basic supervised learning models are insufficient for these tasks and that more sophisticated methods are required to achieve satisfactory performance. For unsupervised learning, we demonstrate that while shallow or basic unsupervised techniques yield limited utility, embedding techniques significantly improve feature representation for DNA. Furthermore, we examine the efficacy of transfer learning using pre-trained protein and natural language models applied to DNA data. Although these approaches offer some benefits, their performance remains suboptimal in comparison to methods specifically designed for DNA sequences.

The metal-insulator transition (MIT) is a captivating phenomenon with broad scientific and practical significance. The surface termination of thin films is crucial for their electronic characteristics, though its specific role in triggering the MIT has not been sufficiently explored. By applying strontium titanate as a substrate to generate a significant out-of-plane strain, we fabricated vanadium sesquioxide (V$$_2$$O$$_3$$) films ranging from 3 to 10 unit cells in thickness. Our analysis of photoemission spectroscopy and transport measurements reveals that the volume is the dominant factor driving the MIT, contrasting with previous findings on bulk crystals where surface termination played a larger role. However, even in these ultrathin structures, surface termination exerts a non-negligible influence on the transition.

A linear space equipped with a bilinear form is known as a metric vector space. Within this framework, the orthogonal complement of a subspace is defined, along with concepts of isotropic, invariant, and fundamental subspaces. Given a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, its dual space $\mathfrak{g}^*$ naturally inherits a Poisson structure derived from the Lie-Poisson bracket. A key challenge in studying dynamical systems defined on such manifolds lies in constructing compatible symplectic leaves. Drawing inspiration from the work of A. Clebsch, this paper introduces and analyzes the process of canonizing Lie-Poisson systems. By utilizing a canonical decomposition involving a basis of $\mathfrak{g}$ and a corresponding coframe in $\mathfrak{g}^*$, we demonstrate that symplectic leaves can be defined as intersections of specific coadjoint orbits with integrals of motion. Furthermore, our findings establish that a geometric integrable structure emerges when a suitable metric is introduced into a Lie-Poisson system.

We introduce the findings of the KMT Net Planetary Anomaly Search (KMPAS) regarding the complete sample of T2 Tidally Driven Orbits (TDO) events from the 2018 observing season's sub-primetime fields. A total of 22 binary microlensing events were identified; however, 11 lacked sufficient data quality for analysis. Of the 11 events that could not be analyzed, 11 showed clear binary characteristics but failed to meet parallax constraints or other criteria for being classified as exoplanets. The remaining 11 events were consistent with the star-binary model rather than the star-planet model. No exoplanets were confirmed in this dataset. We anticipate that future, larger-scale surveys utilizing advanced monitoring techniques will yield more comprehensive results regarding the frequency of exoplanets in the Galactic disk compared to earlier studies.

Building upon our previous study in this series, we develop a unified framework to control the $k$-th order conservation laws within a systematic way. Specifically, we present a control strategy for Navier-Stokes equations by mapping their nonlinearity to an integral equation in $k$-dimensional space and applying our framework to solve a corresponding optimization problem. This methodology yields a set of optimal controls that effectively neutralize both compressible and incompressible nonlinearity across the entire state space. For compressible nonlinearity, this results in a control version of the Navier-Stokes equations that guarantees the existence of a global-in-time solution and ensures the solution remains uniformly bounded. Furthermore, for $3$-$d$ $R$ (though typically $3$-$\text{d}$ incompress) and $2$-$d$ incompress equations, this produces control variants with a solution that is stable over time and uniformly bounded.

This paper introduces a methodology for assessing machine learning models, focusing on two key dimensions: performance and interpretability. To demonstrate the approach, two feature selection strategies—Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, paired with four classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting)—are trained using a No/POPD dataset. A variety of evaluation techniques, including cross-validation and both global and local interpretability via feature significance and SHAP values, are employed to analyze results. The primary contribution is a unified, systematic framework for model selection that balances evaluation and interpretability, validated by applying it to a real-world dataset and highlighting the critical role of feature importance in non-performing loan prediction.

A pair consisting of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and a set of edge weights defines an associated chromatic symmetric function. This work focuses on the specific functions derived from lattice diagrams of Dyck paths within square grids, employing an extended Hahn-poset framework. By utilizing a combinatorial mapping to weighted posets defined on the balls within a quotient of a simplified Young frame, we derive a $q$-analog of a Hahn-poset partition function. This allows for a generating function representation that demonstrates how varying $f_{\Gamma}$ yields a univariate polynomial. Specifically, we calculate this polynomial for "ladder" structures (consisting of two or three rungs) and certain "ladder-like" structures featuring a detour at the apex. We also establish a univariate polynomial for general $l$-rung ladders where all edge weights equal 1. These findings are complemented by several conjectures regarding the chromatic symmetric functions of all graph-ladders.

The emergence of orientation convolutional networks, which natively support both color and orientation inputs, streamlines the training process for orientation-sensitive tasks. By standardizing the training of specific detectors, this framework avoids the complexities and overhead of orientation augmentation and backpropagation through additional layers. Additionally, this approach enhances rotation invariance, significantly boosting performance on classification and detection tasks that must remain consistent across different rotations.

This research investigates linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ twisted by a character through the introduction of a novel relative trace formula, successfully establishing the relative fundamental lemma and facilitating orbital integral comparison. By combining this with Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Wang--Zhang's spectral isolation technique under the relative trace framework, we succeed in formulating a local relative trace formula that computes twisted linear periods. Furthermore, our analysis of key geometric terms within this relative setting allows us to establish a substantial component of Beuzart-Plessis--Wang--Zhang's conjecture, specifically the so-called "first relative trace formula."

We examine the sensitivity of the top quark mass determined from its invariant mass distribution to the presence of light quarks with negligible mass. Our findings indicate that introducing these light quarks via their virtual contributions in the top quark's production—specifically as a quark-antiquark pair—can shift the invariant mass peak by approximately 10 MeV. This represents a significant correction relative to current experimental uncertainties. In contrast, replacing light quarks as they appear in gluon splittings yields a much smaller effect, around 1 MeV.

This paper proves an almost-regular graph with vertex degree $r$ and sequence length $m$ ($1 \leq r \leq m-1$) admits a sequential $m$-edge-coloring. This means the edges can be partitioned into $m$ color classes $E_1, \dots, E_m$ such that every vertex $v$ has degree $r$ within subgraphs $G_i$ formed by edges of color $i$, except for its membership in $E_1$ where it may have degree $r-1$. Consequently, only vertex $v$'s incident edges in $E_1$ result in degree $r-1$, while edges in $E_2$ to $E_m$ remain at degree $r$. This article identifies a necessary and sufficient condition for such graphs to satisfy this property. We also propose algorithmic solutions to determine if such a sequential coloring exists and construct it if it does, and finally, we examine the scenario $r=1$ to establish when a graph $G$ possesses sequential 1-edge-coloring.

This study establishes hypercontractive inequalities associated with weighted Bergman spaces. For a real parameter $\lambda > 0$ and $p$ satisfying the condition $2 \leq p \leq e^{\lambda}$, we investigate the operator $p^{\lambda}$ applied to functions within $L^{\infty}([0,\infty)^{n},\mu)$, mapping it into $L^{p}((\mathbb{R}^{n},\mu))$, where $\mu$ represents a Borel probability measure invariant under translations by the vector $\lambda$. This research extends a previously established result by Boylan to the context of the hypercontractive inequality. Furthermore, when the measure $\mu$ corresponds to a specific form involving exponential terms, we derive an additional hypercontractive inequality.

The ongoing global spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) poses a severe threat to human life. As a highly contagious pathogen capable of rapid transmission, it necessitates swift diagnosis and effective containment strategies. Computed Tomography (CT) serves as a critical diagnostic tool for identifying the disease; however, conducting CT scans on a massive scale is difficult due to the scarcity of specialized equipment and the high cost of trained personnel. Furthermore, standard CT imaging typically requires patients to hold their breath for several seconds, a process that is often unfeasible for those already suffering from respiratory distress caused by the virus. In this study, we introduce a novel two-stage capsule network (CNN) designed to detect coronavirus infections from low-dose CT images, which allow for quicker scanning times (approximately 10–15 seconds) and do not require breath-holding. Specifically, we developed a time-distributed capsule network to analyze dynamic contrast-enhanced CT videos, enabling the model to effectively capture subtle pathological signs associated with the infection. Experimental evaluations indicate that this proposed two-stage approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on available datasets, reaching an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9601 in the first stage and 0.9518 in the second stage.

This study examines future space occupancy projections for Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) using both an analytical approach and Monte Carlo simulations. With the rapid expansion of satellite constellations driven by emerging applications in remote sensing, communications, and navigation, the orbital environment is becoming increasingly congested. This congestion poses significant risks regarding collision avoidance, deorbiting, and the sustainable use of orbital resources. We analyze current and projected LEO usage through these frameworks to quantify the occupancy levels and assess potential risks associated with deploying new satellite constellations. Our findings indicate that LEO is approaching full occupancy, particularly within the critical lower regions below 1,200 kilometers. Consequently, there is a high probability that future satellites will experience extensive orbital congestion and a resulting surge in collision incidents.

The primary challenge in the finite element method (FEM) is the mesh generation process. While high-order coarse meshes are essential for achieving computational efficiency, existing techniques often fail to produce them. This paper introduces an innovative integer linear programming (ILP) approach that effectively addresses this shortcoming. By leveraging the linear line element properties, we construct a novel ILP framework to generate high-order coarse meshes. Comprehensive experiments on CAD models demonstrate that these meshes are accurate, high-order capable, and free of major defects. Furthermore, the mesh generation process is notably faster than comparable approaches.

Moment formulas for correlation coefficients are generated for all possible permutations of the data. By applying the generalized Gessel-Xiao theorem, these formulas are derived for all permutation group elements without the need for the computationally expensive simulation of data arrangements. A key application of these results involves establishing a theoretical framework to calculate the statistical significance of correlation between two vectors of finite length, regardless of the specific values they contain. This theoretical basis is then utilized to empirically evaluate its utility in identifying non-linear correlations, including those observed in the chaos of the Lorenz-Attractor system.

This paper introduces the LitMind Dictionary, a specialized resource offering comprehensive definitions, etymologies, and contextual examples for academic and historical vocabulary. By leveraging advanced natural language processing and machine learning, the system enhances its descriptive capabilities with synonyms, semantic contexts, and tailored Vectors for pertinent word associations. To support future expansion and research, the codebase has been made fully open-source.

Explainable recommendation systems have garnered significant attention in academic research, driven by a desire to understand recommendation rationales and enhance user adherence to them. However, a critical gap remains regarding how explanations themselves should be explained to truly increase compliance. This study investigates explanation constancy—a key dimension where explanations for the same user remain consistent across time—as a driver for adherence within LIME-RS, a popular explanation framework for recommendations. Through extensive experiments, the research demonstrates that LIME-RS generated explanations exhibit a high degree of long-term constancy and that this consistency is directly linked to increased user adherence. Consequently, the work underscores the necessity for explanation generators to prioritize constancy, alongside other attributes, to build more reliable explanation-based recommendation systems.

We introduce a comprehensive theoretical framework for InAs quantum wells situated near SiGe interfaces, which elucidates the origins of Fermi level pinning (FLP) and demonstrates that it can be regulated. This near-surface configuration generates a unique, additional polarization field that acts in concert with the built-in polarization field, resulting from the mismatch between InAs quantum wells and the surrounding Si matrix. This interaction produces a novel polarization effect that effectively counteracts the internal field, allowing the position of the Fermi level in InAs-to-SiGe heterostructures to be shifted. This mechanism is demonstrated through analysis of band alignments and the origins of FLP in both isolated InAs/SiGe and integrated InAs/SiGe structures containing GaOx/SiGe barrier layers. This mechanism is demonstrated through analysis of band alignments and the origins of FLP in both isolated InAs/SiGe and integrated InAs/SiGe structures containing GaOx/SiGe barrier layers.

This study investigates the robust learning of concept classes over the framework of probabilistic model checking, focusing on the utility of queries and their interplay with specific data distributions. While previous research established robust learnability without queries for certain concept classes, this work examines how local queries can enhance sample efficiency for a set of classes previously only learnable with excessive samples. Specifically, it demonstrates that with access to local queries, these classes achieve polynomial sample complexity under every reasonable distribution, provided the query tolerance is sufficiently small. Additionally, the work explores the converse scenario, analyzing the limitations of local queries in achieving polynomial sample complexity for broader, non-restricted concept classes. The paper concludes by presenting a framework to determine the query sample complexity of any given concept class relative to various threshold distances and divergence measures.

Building on our prior work regarding fast and accurate synthetic data generation for benchmarking OT algorithms, this study investigates the complexity of solving the optimal transport problem between two fully triangular matrices, including cases with inexact solutions. While the general OT problem scales cubically with the number of pixels, this paper presents two solutions: the first leverages the Sinkhorn-Normalized algorithm, and the second exploits matrix properties to reduce the problem to a series of one-dimensional operations. Consequently, the computational cost drops to $O(N)$ for both, where the parameter $e \in [0,1)$ indicates the acceptable error threshold. Notably, this efficient algorithm also functions correctly when the cost matrix is defined by the Euclidean distance metric.

This study reports on FUV observations of the active M-dwarf AU Microscopii, acquired by the Cosmic Background Explorer satellite during both quiescent and eruptive phases. The data indicate that UV flares on this star are more frequent and possess higher energies than previously identified in the optical spectrum. Specifically, X-ray, FUV, and optical flares occur with a recurrence interval of roughly 1.5 hours, whereas two events were detected simultaneously in X-ray and FUV, while none were recorded in the optical. Analysis of the FUV flare evolution reveals a rise time of approximately 10 minutes and a decay duration of 1.5 hours. Additionally, UV emission from flares persists for several days, although at a level below quiescent emission. The study further examines the impact of stellar activity on the two known exoplanets orbiting this star. By quantifying the additional radiation received from flares, quiescent UV output, and optical emission, we calculate that AU Mic b and c are subjected to significantly greater heating than predicted for a typical M-dwarf, a dynamic environment that could influence atmospheric stability and potentially render the planets uninhabitable.

We examine the impact of a continuous medium on the motion of a charged particle subjected to an external field, focusing on the analogy between an external medium and self-action caused by radiation. While previous studies assumed that such a medium is at rest or in motion relative to the particle, resulting in a friction-like force, we propose a new model where the medium is resistive. In this resistive scenario, energy transfer to the medium mimics the complex self-force structure produced by accelerating the particle through the medium. We derive an equation of motion incorporating this medium effect and an associated "generalized radiation back-reaction" term that extends the standard Abraham-Dirac-Lorentz-Landau-Lifshitz force. Notably, this equation eliminates the pathological "runaway" solutions characteristic of the original formulation without requiring perturbation theory.

In classification scenarios where training data is imbalanced, standard discriminative methods like nearest neighbors often fail to achieve optimal results. This paper proposes a statistical strategy to address such imbalance, specifically tailored for nearest neighbor classifiers. By deriving a classification function grounded in hypothesis testing, the approach enables classes to compete equitably, with error rates for minority and majority groups being balanced. Empirical evaluations on nearest neighbor systems applied to the Emotion Recognition in Speech dataset indicate that this statistical method surpasses conventional baselines, including re-sampling techniques and other known statistical methods. Furthermore, findings reveal a nuanced trade-off: while re-sampling boosts overall accuracy, it often disproportionately harms minority class performance, whereas our proposed statistical method enhances accuracy across both majority and minority classes simultaneously.

We present a new ultra-luminous quasar sample identified through the SkyMapper Full-Sky Survey, featuring 13 new quasar redshifts greater than 0.7. These discoveries were isolated by flagging bright sources with the quasar probability (QPRO) greater than 0.7 and subsequently cross-referencing them with existing spectral line redshift databases. The resulting sample includes seven new ultra-UV luminous quasar candidates (QULs) with bolometric luminosities exceeding $10^{34}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The combined dataset of 26 quasar candidates at $z > 0.7$ and $L > L_{10^{34}}$ represents a complete set of quasar candidates brighter than $10^{34}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at $z > 0.7$ identified through SkyMapper. The estimated completeness of this sample is at least 90%, and its magnitude completeness is 95%. We have calculated the luminosity function for these quasar candidates at $z > 0.7$ and $L > L_{10^{34}}$ using the maximum likelihood estimator. The derived luminosity function is consistent with previous measurements from $14.5 < z < 20$ UV luminous quasar candidates ($L > L_{10^{34}}$ UV), but exhibits a factor of 2.5 discrepancy

This paper presents an experimental investigation into the tunneling dynamics of electrons and superconducting Cooper pairs between a semiconductor quantum dot and a superconducting island. By utilizing the quantum dot itself as a sensitive detector for charges moving from the island, we have mapped out the relevant tunneling pathways. Our findings demonstrate that even in conditions where direct electron tunneling is suppressed, significant movement of Cooper pairs remains observable.

This work examines the contraction property of entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws with respect to the $L_1$ norm. By utilizing cross-contraction principles to establish bounds on the distances between such solutions, we derive sufficient conditions under which contractions hold. These findings validate and expand upon the contraction framework for the Euler equations in gas dynamics as previously suggested in \cite{BKLW}. Additionally, a boundary value scenario is analyzed, where the application of contraction arguments successfully proves the uniqueness of contraction stable boundary value solutions.

The challenge of creating infinite novel perspectives from a single image remains unresolved. Existing techniques typically rely on a predetermined maximum frame rate in video models, forcing a fixed sampling interval for polygon mesh reconstruction, and struggle to maintain smooth transitions for freely chosen perspectives. We introduce DiffDreamer, an approach grounded in conditional diffusion techniques that enables the generation of unlimited novel viewpoints from a single input image. Furthermore, our strategy ensures smooth transitions between frames during the trajectory planning phase within the generative model. We enhance this capability by training the network on video models capable of handling variable frame rates and by implementing a generative model-specific temporal noise scheduling mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods regarding both generative quality and stability.

This work introduces a straightforward framework designed to forecast and regulate the dynamics of complex systems of coupled processes. Specifically, it addresses networks where individual processes are non-linear and where inter-process interactions depend on arbitrary parameters. The proposed solution employs a purely data-driven approach, utilizing the graph structure for prediction and optimization while requiring no specific knowledge of the process dynamics. Instead, it relies solely on historical data collected from a limited subset of nodes. The method's validity regarding both its capability to predict system evolution and its ability to implement feedback control is substantiated by theoretical guarantees, supported by numerical simulations and an application to a networked Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model.

The instability development within a liquid film coating a cylindrical fiber is examined with a specific focus on how surface slip influences stability characteristics. A theoretical framework is established that models this instability as an extension of the standard Rayleigh-Plateau problem, adapted for a circumference constraint. This theory predicts that slip significantly accelerates the $2\pi/\kappa$-mode growth rate while simultaneously causing a shift in the most unstable wavelength toward larger values compared to a no-slip scenario. These findings align well with observations from experiments involving benzene on glass fibers, where neon-dense gas environments minimized evaporative losses.

This research investigates how small perturbations in the initial data of solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation influence their subsequent $C^1_{\text{loc}}$ solutions on $[0,T)$, where $T$ is the maximal time of existence. By utilizing the theory of pseudo-differential operators and establishing novel commutation and Lipschitz-type inequalities, the study achieves the following key results:

1.  If the initial data is sufficiently close in a weighted $H^2_{\text{loc}}$ sense, the resulting $C^1_{\text{loc}}$ solutions remain close in a weighted $C^2_{\text{loc}}$ framework up to blow-up time.
2.  If the initial data is a small perturbation in $H^1$ with respect to a fixed reference solution, the two solutions remain close in a $C^1_{\text{loc}}$ framework throughout the interval $[0,T)$.

These theorems are novel to the existing analysis of the Hunter-Saxton equation.

Colposcopy-based ultrasound (CUS) offers a rapid and non-invasive method for scoliosis diagnosis and monitoring. This study evaluates the feasibility of using robots to operate ultrasound scanners for scoliosis assessment, focusing on achieving high inter-scan reliability and detecting curvature beyond 10°. The scoliosis curve was evaluated using a handheld probe on 30 participants by three distinct operators: a robotic agent, a physician, and a nurse, with each performing two consecutive scans per participant. The primary endpoints assessed the inter-reproducibility and inter-compatibility of maximal vertical lumbar distance (VLL) and maximal apical angle (MAA) measurements. A fixed-effect meta-analysis on MAAs measured 10 cm from the vertebra exhibiting the greatest deviation (T10-M10A) was conducted to compare consistency across operators. In total, 85.7% of all CUS measurements recorded a positive angle, indicating the presence of spinal curvature. While the comparison between the physician and patient showed significant similarity (P > 0.05), CUS performed by nurses or the robot demonstrated a statistically significant difference (P < 0.05). Notably, CUL acquired by operators (physician and nurse) exhibited higher sensitivity for detecting spinal curvature >10° than did the robotic process. These findings indicate that, although CUL performed by medical professionals shows greater similarity to robotic scans, human-collected data demonstrates superior inter-reproducibility and diagnostic sensitivity.

This study introduces a novel methodology for creating artificial speech duration data, designed to enhance the robustness of speech recognition systems when encountering out-of-distribution duration samples during training. The proposed approach calculates the median duration for each word from a corpus of real speech and aggregates these values by phonetic transcriptions to produce a continuous probability distribution. This distribution serves to extend or lengthen original word durations based on real talker variability without adding noise, effectively replacing simple scaling strategies that extend duration by repeating phoneme units or adding time increments. Experiments conducted on two datasets—TCD-TIMIT and Librispeech—demonstrate that applying this new method improves performance for models processing generated data containing variable durations and out-of-distribution cases, resulting in WER reductions of 12.5% and 5.6% on TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-TCD-T

This study introduces a new approach to detecting hate speech. A proposed solution involves training models using the TF-IDF technique to extract linguistic features from data obtained via the dataset. The research evaluates the best performing model by analyzing its accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-Score. The results indicate that the suggested method achieves an F1-score of 86.66% on the "HateXb dataset."

This study introduces a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) framework designed for joint optimization of point clouds and 2D images through the shared processing of features via a MIMO convolutional network. Initially, a two-stage strategy was implemented: at the feature extraction stage, two separate networks handled paired data streams, followed by a stage of feature sharing using cross-stage connections to integrate this information. While effective, this approach was constrained by the high computational costs of maintaining two distinct networks and the inefficiencies inherent in the early phase of feature sharing. To overcome these drawbacks, we developed an advanced single-stage MIMO architecture capable of performing feature sharing during the initial network iterations. This modification not only eliminated the need for duplicate networks but also allowed those sharing operations to occur over sparser, earlier features, resulting in a substantially more efficient system.

This survey provides a comprehensive review of public datasets designed for the domain of historical document image analysis. It categorizes, organizes, and examines the strengths and limitations of these collections, covering the full spectrum from handwriting analysis to historical printing. Furthermore, the work outlines standard preprocessing techniques employed to prepare both manuscript and printed material for computer processing, offering researchers and scholars an invaluable resource to facilitate future research in historical document analysis.

Industrial robots are frequently employed for high-speed and high-precision tasks, yet their drive mechanisms often suffer from inherent nonlinearities, leading to vibration and position errors alongside low dynamic stiffness. This paper investigates the implementation of flatness-based control to enhance trajectory tracking fidelity and precision by utilizing secondary encoders found on a robot's joints. This approach involves integrating measured acceleration data—second derivatives of position—to redesign the control law. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, the paper presents a novel flatness-based control law law to evaluate, it introduces a nonlinear robotic dynamics simulator capable of accurately modeling the dynamics within an industrial setting. A comparison is then made between this simulator and experimental results obtained from an actual robotic arm to assess the performance improvements. Results indicate that utilizing feedback loop acceleration significantly diminishes trajectory tracking errors, thereby elevating execution precision.

Chronic diseases are characterized by intricate health trajectories that involve simultaneous changes across multiple physiological domains. This study examines whether a data-driven approach utilizing multiple simultaneous time-to-event models can identify a finite set of latent states within these trajectories. The proposed method extends the Cox mixture model by incorporating the correlated, multivariate nature of life health trajectories, specifically accounting for the censored, censored, and censored nature of the data. The results indicate that the method can identify latent classes with distinct time-to-event probabilities. Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on updating a minimal subset of parameters in pre-trained models to adapt them for downstream tasks, offering an attractive alternative to full model fine-tuning. This work explores whether this strategy can be effectively realized by assigning dedicated special tokens, such as [EOS], specific roles in generating labels for sequence tasks like classification. By introducing the concept of the Special Token Adapter, the research demonstrates how these generation-area special tokens facilitate learning task-specific features while maintaining the extensive pre-trained language model's general capabilities. The study analyzes the efficacy of this technique across various tasks, including in-domain and cross-domain settings. Results indicate that across tasks like sequence classification, sequence tagging, and sequence generation, this approach achieves performance on par with, or superior to, existing parameter-efficient techniques. Furthermore, it delivers a significant advantage over other such techniques specifically in the context of sequence classification.

This study examines the connections between dynamic and thermodynamic properties in a generic weakly polydisperse polymer melt using molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, we investigate how dynamic structural order and disorder, represented by order parameter distributions, connect to both dynamic and thermodynamic relaxation times. For a wide range of cooling rates, the time distribution for structural reconfiguration scales with the Debye-Stokes-Einstein timescale, revealing that thermodynamic and dynamic non-Debye-Stokes-Einstein violations emerge in systems with high molecular mass. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative relationship linking relaxation times to thermodynamic free volume and configurational free energy density distributions. Our findings demonstrate that the thermodynamic time scale derived from the free energy density distribution correlates universally across different molecular weights, even under varying cooling rates. Additionally, we explore the thermodynamic underpinnings of dynamic heterogeneity by correlating relaxation times with spatial distributions of local thermodynamic and thermodynamic free energy densities.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing have seen a surge in research regarding language models' capacity to handle linguistic negation. While empirical studies suggest current capabilities are constrained by data, this study represents a systematic investigation into how transformer-based models manage negation across different contexts, with a specific focus on developmental negation. Findings indicate that although models struggle with negative queries, they possess some ability to perform appropriately in non-challenging scenarios. Furthermore, this work introduces a new benchmark for evaluating model performance in transformer negation handling, featuring 16 carefully curated datasets that cover the full developmental timeline of negation.

Attention mechanisms have become integral to neural machine translation, yet recent research indicates a tendency for models to align excessively with the beginning of the input sentence. To counter this, this paper introduces a novel look-ahead component that models the relationship between the remaining, future part of the target sentence and the current output token being generated. Experiments conducted on the German-English and Vietnamese-English translation tasks reveal that combining the proposed look-ahead module with standard attention mechanisms yields improved translation metrics. Notably, these models exhibit more uniform attention distribution patterns compared to baseline systems.

We establish this result using the representation of non-local semigroups alongside a specific variant of Kotelenez's theorem for differential equations. Features in the primordial power spectrum can influence predictions for cosmological observables, potentially acting as a signal of new physics. While standard mechanisms for generating such features often require modifications to the physics occurring at the same scales, the classical cosmological collider offers an alternative approach by creating them during a period where acceleration halts. This scenario, which occurs when a classical turning point emerges in the equation of state, allows to produce features that probe physics occurring at vastly different energy levels. This work investigates a scenario where two massive fields with distinct masses interact with a scalar inflaton; although these fields cannot be excited directly due to their masses, their effects manifest as oscillations in the scalar power spectrum during the transition from deceleration to acceleration. These induced wiggles correspond to the cosmological collider signatures generated at the transition point. The frequency of the resulting oscillations is determined by the masses of the interacting fields, and their amplitudes depend on the masses and self-interaction strengths of the inflaton. The analysis also examines how the inflaton's potential influences the amplitude of the oscillations. Finally, the paper connects these large-scale features to their impact on the CMB power spectrum, specifically regarding scalar perturbations and the tensor-to-scalar ratio.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely employed for object classification tasks, yet their internal mechanisms remain difficult to interpret. While prior research has attempted to visualize convolutional filter weights to understand the network's processing stages, this study proposes generating more informative filters by integrating them with a latent visual-semantic layer. This approach relies on the assumption that filters within these intermediate layers encode semantic information. By examining the correlation between the input image and the activation of each filter across its spatial dimensions, we derive visual-filter attention maps that serve as an interpretive tool for the model's reasoning processes.

This study investigates the role of longitudinal phonons in a single-chain cuprate model characterized by both electron-phonon and spin-phonon-coupling mechanisms. Our analysis reveals that phonons generate an extended, electron-mediated attractive force between neighbors. We demonstrate that the strength of this phonon-driven attraction surpasses the conventional Coulomb repulsion across the entire spectrum of electron densities. Furthermore, the associated effective one-particle dispersion exhibits significant renormalization, with the system's overall attraction scaling proportionally to the square of the electron-phonon coupling constant ($e^2$). Notably, even in the absence of long-range Coulomb interactions, these Coulomb-independent attractive forces can sustain a robust antiferromagnetic state. Additionally, the combined influence of electron-electlectron and spin-dependent couplings on both the lattice and superlattice phonon modes results in complex renormalization of the phonon spectra.

The MPHIA (Multi-Purpose Household and Individual Surveys Initiative) initiative aggregates various survey datasets to create a unified data framework. This study utilizes causal structure learning to examine the cause-and-effect relationships within the individual-level data from these surveys. Specifically, we use a Bayesian approach to construct a causal acyclic graphical model, which allows for the inference of causal structures and parameter estimation. By applying these methods to the latest 2018 Ethiopia household survey data, we identify causal pathways linking individual health outcomes, wealth levels, and education levels. This analysis supports decision-makers in Ethiopia by enhancing their capacity to design and refine public health policies.

High-dimensional dynamic factor models are examined in this paper, with emphasis on recent advancements from both contemporary statistical and economic research. A selective overview of the theoretical and empirical foundations for dynamic factor and principal component models is established to introduce the subject. The paper subsequently surveys the leading-edge literature, analyzing how various estimation techniques and testing methodologies are applied to these models. Potential extensions and necessary avenues for extending these models are also examined. Furthermore, empirical investigations are conducted by comparing leading estimators using Monte Carlo simulations, and the performance of these methods is evaluated by applying them to actual data.

The Nikaidô-Isoda-Fan inequality defines an equilibrium problem that encompasses optimization problems, variational inequalities, the Kakutani fixed point, Nash equilibria, and more, all as specific instances. In this study, a method for determining a fixed point associated with the equilibrium problem is introduced, featuring the necessary property of being skew. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the set of fixed points corresponds exactly to the set of solutions to said problem. An applicable framework is also established, proving that, under specific conditions, the presence limit points for the sequence generated by the algorithm guarantees actual convergence. Finally, several novel approaches to addressing both the equilibrium problem and the intersection of multiple sets of solutions are proposed and examined.

Recent findings have demonstrated the effectiveness of using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and other machine learning models for steganography, specifically by embedding secret data into the statistical micro-patterns of cover files like images. However, a critical challenge remains: determining a reliable method to extract the hidden data from the modified media. This study introduces a novel approach utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) to achieve reversible steganography. In this framework, a GAN is employed to embed secret data into the statistical micro-patterns of the image, while a BNN serves as the complementary detector/capability for both identifying the presence of hidden information and precisely locating the necessary adjustments to the media. Uniquely, this BNN-driven approach facilitates a fully reversible steganographic process, effectively eliminating the risk of introducing a detectable "steganostic" footprint to the final data.

The study examines the influence of turbulent phenomena on dynamo mechanisms within rapidly rotating, stratified flows, utilizing mean-field modeling. By integrating three-dimensional numerical simulations as the foundational data for the mean-field approach, the research reveals that turbulent diffusion and convection-driven turbulent conduction are essential to reproduce the observed global dynamo. Specifically, these two factors are required to generate the magnetic structures necessary for the dynamo to function. Consequently, turbulent effects must be fully accounted for in both mean-field modeling and subsequent theoretical analyses.

We have conducted ALMA observations of the nuclear molecular outflow in the galaxy NGC4945, utilizing a 1.2 mm CO(3-2) line map alongside complementary 88 GHz sub-mm continuum imaging. Our CO data reveal a complex outflow structure featuring a high-velocity component extending several hundred parsecs in a torus-like shape, alongside a low-velocity component spanning roughly 1000 parsecs. We identify a central dense core within this structure that exhibits CO emission at velocities of $\pm 100$ km/s relative to the galaxy's systemic velocity. This core is situated approximately 100 pc from the nuclear starburst, a location that likely corresponds to a circumnuclear ring. Multi-wavelength data indicate that the nuclear starburst drives winds in opposite directions, which are then chocked by this ring, resulting in high-velocity emission. Additionally, we detect CO(3-2) line emission at low velocities (approximately 10--20 km/s) within a 100 pc radius of the galaxy's center. This suggests the presence of a massive inflow of cold gas that is being funneled into the nuclear region, potentially nourishing the nuclear starburst and outflow dynamics.

This research focuses on the numerical solution of a quasilinear diffusion model tailored for magnetized plasmas. The mathematical framework is reduced to a system of coupled one-dimensional hyperbolic balance equations. We introduce a mixed finite element method combined with Galerkin discretization to solve the resulting algebraic hyperbolic balance system. This method offers several distinct advantages: it conserves mass in the discrete setting, maintains the non-negativity of distribution and flux functions, and critically, ensures the conservation of entropy. The latter property, which is crucial for guaranteeing convergence, is achieved through the use of minimum and maximum flux upwind schemes. Additionally, an efficient and robust solution strategy for the nonlinear minimum and maximum operators is developed. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated via two numerical examples. The first example mimics the quasilinear diffusion model for Langmuir waves interacting with an electron beam, utilizing the entropy-conservation property to validate the robustness of the approach. The second example extends these findings to the case of ion cyclotron waves acting upon minor ions.

Second derivative implicit methods (SDIMSIMs) are distinguished by their high order accuracy and exceptional stability across all complex planes. Nevertheless, order reduction often renders them impractical for solving stiff ordinary differential equations. This article introduces a variable stepsize algorithm to mitigate step degradation, employing the difference between two successive approximations to compute an a posteriori error estimate. A posteriori error estimates inform a variable integrator, which is then compared to the standard uniform-step method. The paper provides the derived formulas for these methods, establishes their properties, and demonstrates their utility through illustrative numerical studies.
